nameStory: The 'broad-leaved' part of this plant's name comes from its distinctively wide leaflets compared to other sweet peas in the region. It's called 'sweet pea' because it belongs to the same genus as the fragrant garden sweet pea, though this wild cousin has much less noticeable scent. The 'everlasting' nickname refers to its perennial nature and incredibly long blooming season that can stretch for months.
description: Broad-leaved sweet pea is a vigorous climbing vine that sprawls and scrambles over fences, walls, and other plants using its curling tendrils. This robust perennial can reach 6-9 feet long, creating dense tangles of stems covered in pink to magenta pea-like flowers. The plant produces distinctive winged stems and broad, oval leaflets that help distinguish it from other climbing vines. Originally from Europe, it has naturalized throughout New England and blooms prolifically from summer into fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright pink to magenta pea-shaped flowers cluster in groups of 4-10 on long stalks. Each flower has the classic 'butterfly' shape with a large upper petal (standard), two side petals (wings), and a lower keel, and they're about an inch across with little to no fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Each leaf has just two broad, oval leaflets (1-3 inches long) that feel smooth and slightly waxy to the touch. The leaflets are much wider than other sweet peas, and each leaf ends in a branched, curly tendril that wraps around supports.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A vigorous climbing vine that uses curling tendrils to scramble over supports, creating dense tangles. The stems are distinctly flattened and winged - run your finger along them and you'll feel the thin, papery ridges.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces flat, brown seed pods about 3-4 inches long that split open when ripe with a satisfying 'pop' to release hard, round seeds. The pods start green and papery, turning brown and brittle as they mature.

habitat: Look for broad-leaved sweet pea along roadsides, old fence lines, and disturbed areas where it can climb on structures or scramble over banks. It thrives in sunny spots with well-drained soil and is especially common near old homesteads, abandoned gardens, and along railroad tracks. This adaptable plant tolerates poor soils and drought once established.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from perennial roots, and the distinctive winged stems with broad leaflets make identification possible even before flowering begins.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with clusters of bright pink flowers appearing continuously. This is the best time for identification when flowers, leaves, and climbing habit are all clearly visible.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming into early fall while seed pods mature and split open. Late fall brings yellowing foliage before the above-ground portions die back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving only dried stems and scattered seed pods. The perennial roots remain alive underground, ready to sprout again in spring.

funFact: Despite being called a 'sweet pea,' this plant's seeds are actually mildly toxic and can cause a condition called lathyrism if eaten regularly - a far cry from edible garden peas! The plant compensates for this by being incredibly generous with its flowers, sometimes blooming continuously for over four months straight.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with garden sweet pea (Lathyrus odoratus), but broad-leaved sweet pea has much wider leaflets, winged stems you can feel with your fingers, and flowers with little scent. Remember: if it smells sweet and has narrow leaves, it's probably the garden variety; if it has wide leaves and winged stems, you've found the broad-leaved species.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - this 'sweet pea' is quite different from both edible garden peas and the fragrant sweet peas sold at florists. While it shares the family resemblance of pea-shaped flowers, it's purely ornamental and mildly toxic. The confusion comes from early botanists grouping similar-looking plants together before understanding their relationships.
compareHints: Among New England's sweet peas, broad-leaved sweet pea stands out with its distinctly wide leaflets - most others like meadow pea have narrow, grass-like leaflets. The winged stems are also unique; run your finger along a seaside pea or marsh pea stem and you won't feel those papery ridges. Its robust, sprawling growth habit and long bloom season also set it apart from the more delicate native species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Lathyrus species, seaside pea is the only one with those distinctive thick, waxy blue-green leaves and strict beach habitat.
Among New England's wild peas, narrow-leaved everlasting-pea stands out with its bold pink flowers and strongly winged stems.
Among New England's wild peas, meadow pea stands out with its bright yellow flowers - most of its relatives like seaside pea and marsh pea have purple or pink blooms.
Among its Lathyrus relatives, marsh pea is distinguished by its wetland habitat and pinkish-purple flowers.

Unlike the broad-leaved sweet pea which has wider leaflets and no tubers, or the seaside pea which has 6-12 leaflets, tuberous pea is distinguished by its simple two-leaflet arrangement and underground tuber system.
Unlike its Lathyrus relatives in New England, spring vetch lacks the climbing tendrils found on species like broad-leaved sweet pea and narrow-leaved everlasting-pea.
Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, sweet pea stands out for its incredible fragrance and annual growth habit.

Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, pale vetchling stands out for its uniquely subdued flower color – while seaside pea has purple flowers, meadow pea is bright yellow, and broad-leaved sweet pea shows off in magenta.
Grass pea stands out from its New England Lathyrus cousins primarily by its unique brick-red flowers - no other sweet pea or vetchling in our region shares this color.
